materials.name: Reed fibre
materials.notes: Retted in standing water until the pith rots away, then combed out and dried. The whole delta runs on it -- matting, basketry, and every rope that does not need to hold a boat.

materials.name: Palm husk
materials.notes: The coarse mat of fibre at the base of a frond. Harsher than reed and far more patient of salt water, which is why the harbour rope is husk and the house rope is reed.

materials.name: Cliff-goat hair
materials.notes: Combed from the winter coat rather than shorn. Spins into a yarn that stays warm wet, which matters more on the Vindhya than anything else about it.

materials.name: Bast
materials.notes: The inner bark, stripped in long ribbons and beaten soft. Taken from a tree the taker intends to keep, so it is cut in bands and never a ring.

materials.name: Iron-teak timber
materials.notes: Canon already records this tree for ship timber and tower beams, which is a strong claim about a wood: it means the grain holds under a load that would split anything else growing near it.

materials.name: Mangrove pole
materials.notes: Cut from the stilt roots rather than the trunk. Already the right shape, already used to standing in salt water, and no use at all for anything that must be straight.

materials.name: Bamboo cane
materials.notes: Two classes, honestly. A whole cane is a scaffold pole; a split one is a strap. Canon records the grove for scaffolding, rafts and tools, which is all three uses of one plant.

materials.name: Sandalwood billet
materials.notes: Heartwood only; the sapwood is scentless and worth nothing. Carved, burnt or ground, and canon has it doing all three.

materials.name: Leviathan bone
materials.notes: Canon states outright that the hide and bone plate of the Abyssal Blue are harvested for building maritime vessels. A single rib is a keel. Nobody takes one alone, and nobody takes one often.

materials.name: Antler
materials.notes: Shed each year and gathered off the ground, which makes it the one bone in this list that costs nothing but the walking.

materials.name: Boar tusk
materials.notes: Curved, hollow at the root, and hard enough to take an edge. Worn as often as it is worked.

materials.name: Sawfish bone
materials.notes: The rostral teeth of the sawfish come out of the estuary already barbed, and a harpoon made from one is a harpoon somebody did very little to.

materials.name: Goat hide
materials.notes: Tanned with bark liquor. Becomes a water-skin, a drum head, or the seat of a saddle, in roughly that order of frequency.

materials.name: Croc hide
materials.notes: Scuted, awkward to cut and nearly impossible to wear out. The dromedary-croc's is the lighter of the two and the one the delta actually uses.

materials.name: Sinew
materials.notes: Filed under hide as well as fibre because of how it is got: skinning, not retting. Dries to a lashing that tightens as it goes, which no plant fibre does.

materials.name: Oyster shell
materials.notes: Burnt for lime, ground for temper, or cut for inlay. The middens outside Dwarka are made of the ones nobody bothered with.

materials.name: Ammonite shell
materials.notes: Canon inlays the Board of the Chess of Fate with fossilised ammonites, so this is a material with a reputation before it is a material with a use. The black ones are not worked by anybody sensible.

materials.name: Crayfish carapace
materials.notes: Thin, blue, and worth keeping only for the colour. Ground into a pigment more often than it is worked whole.

materials.name: Frankincense
materials.notes: Canon already records the scrub for incense and trade resin. Tapped by scoring the bark and coming back a fortnight later, which makes it a crop as much as a gathering.

materials.name: Myrrh gum
materials.notes: The wound salve canon names on the myrrh-thorn is this, softened in oil. It is also the best glue in the desert, which is the same property read two ways.

materials.name: Pitch
materials.notes: Boiled down from resinous heartwood in a covered pit. Nothing floats without it -- every hull in canon is a hull somebody paid this attention. Boiled out of resinous heartwood in a covered pit.

materials.name: River clay
materials.notes: Dug from the cut bank where the water has already done the sorting. The Saraswati's is grey wet and buff fired.

materials.name: Grog
materials.notes: Old fired pots, crushed and put back into new clay so the new one survives the kiln. The only material in this file that can only be made from itself. Crushed out of old fired pots. There is no grog in the ground.

materials.name: Flint
materials.notes: Nodules out of limestone, or cobbles out of a riverbed. Knaps predictably, which is the entire reason it outlasted better-looking stone.

materials.name: Basalt
materials.notes: The Deccan is made of it. Too tough to knap and perfect for anything that must grind -- querns, mortars, and the Board of the Chess of Fate.

materials.name: Sandstone
materials.notes: Dressed rather than knapped. Soft enough to cut with bronze and hard enough to still be standing when the person who cut it is not.

materials.name: Magma-glass
materials.notes: Volcanic glass, and canon's Chess of Fate has its squares inlaid with it. Takes an edge sharper than bronze and loses it to a hard look.

materials.name: Scar glass
materials.notes: Fused sand from the Glass Scar at Dwarka. Whatever made it is one of the things the player is there to work out, so canon says what it is and pointedly not how it happened.

materials.name: Native copper
materials.notes: Found as metal rather than smelted from ore -- green-crusted lumps in a dry watercourse. Cold-worked, annealed, worked again.

materials.name: Tin ore
materials.notes: Cassiterite, heavy and black, panned out of highland gravel. Scarce enough that its trade route is more important than its deposit.

materials.name: Bronze
materials.notes: Copper and tin, and the era's outer edge. Canon is a bronze world with iron as a rumour; nothing here should let a recipe quietly invent a smelted iron industry. Cast, never found. Copper and tin and a furnace -- see recipe_cast_bronze.

materials.name: Salt crust
materials.notes: Scraped off a pan in sheets. It is preservative, currency and the ground Dwarka stands on, which is why it is its own class and not a footnote under stone.

materials.name: Natron
materials.notes: The bitter salt from a dry lake bed. Cleans, cures hide, and makes glass possible.

materials.name: Indigo
materials.notes: Fermented in a vat until it stinks, then oxidised in the air. The cloth comes out green and turns blue while you watch, which is why it is worth what it is worth.

materials.name: Red ochre
materials.notes: Iron-stained earth, ground and washed. The oldest pigment anybody has, and the one every mark in this world is made in until somebody wants blue.

materials.name: Lamp black
materials.notes: Soot caught on a cold plate held over a flame. Bound with gum it is ink, which makes it the material Varuna's diary is actually written in. Soot caught on a plate. Nobody gathers it; somebody makes it.

materials.name: Red delta rice
materials.notes: Canon records it as a staple grain and a trade good. Stores through a season, which is the whole difference between a camp and a settlement.

materials.name: Lotus-root taro
materials.notes: A flood crop in canon's own words -- it wants the water the rice cannot take, so the two together mean a bad year is survivable.

materials.name: Dates
materials.notes: Dried on the frond and carried in a pressed block. Sweet, heavy, and the reason a desert crossing is arithmetic rather than a gamble.

materials.name: Tamarind pulp
materials.notes: Canon files the tree under food, souring agent and shade. This is the first two; the third is not a thing you can carry.

materials.name: River fish
materials.notes: Split, salted and dried on a rack. Named for what it is rather than for a species, because a weir does not sort its catch.

materials.name: Mahua oil
materials.notes: Pressed from the seed. Canon already has the tree down for oil, a fermented drink and a ritual offering, and this is only the first of the three.

materials.name: Charcoal
materials.notes: Canon names the ghost mangrove for charcoal specifically. Burnt slow under turf, and the only fuel in this list hot enough to melt anything. Burnt slow under turf from timber. Not a thing lying about.

materials.name: Dung cake
materials.notes: Patted flat and dried on a wall. Unglamorous, universal, and what almost every meal in this world is actually cooked over.

materials.name: Neem bark
materials.notes: Canon has the tree for medicine and insect repellent. Bitter enough that nobody takes it for pleasure and reliable enough that everybody has some.

materials.name: Shilajit
materials.notes: The tonic canon names on the creeper -- a mineral exudate scraped from high rock. Filed as physic rather than salt because of what it is for, not what it is made of.

materials.name: Bitter greens
materials.notes: Fourteen leaves, and the number is the point rather than the plants. Gathered on one morning from ditch, bund, pond and field edge, most of them things nobody planted. Bitter to the last, on purpose.

materials.name: Ginger
materials.notes: Dug rather than picked. Keeps a season in dry sand and travels as well as anything that is not a stone, which is most of why it is worth as much away from where it grows.

materials.name: Mustard seed
materials.notes: Pressed for a hot yellow oil, or cracked whole into it. A field of mustard is two crops standing in one place.

materials.name: Cardamom
materials.notes: Three pods will scent a whole pot, which is the only reason something growing in wet shade on one plateau is eaten a thousand miles away.

materials.name: Mango
materials.notes: Two crops from one tree a month apart: the green fruit is the sour one cooks with, and the ripe one is not cooked at all.

materials.name: Jackfruit
materials.notes: Unripe it is cooked like meat and ripe it is eaten like sweets. Canon files it as produce both times, because it is a fruit whichever way it is used.

materials.name: Kuchla seed
materials.notes: Flat grey discs, kept in a sealed jar and counted. Nothing is made of them but medicine, and that only after a fortnight of soaking.

materials.name: Purified kuchla
materials.notes: What a fortnight of soaking leaves. Still measured in single seeds and still counted out, because the process removes the danger rather than the need for care.

materials.name: Dhatura seed
materials.notes: Kept for the shrine and never for the pot. Canon records no preparation that makes these safe, and the households that grow it do not look for one.

materials.name: Aconite root
materials.notes: The most dangerous thing in canon's ground, and the only poison it records being used as a weapon -- on arrows, by hill people, once.

materials.name: Ashwagandha root
materials.notes: Dug in the dry months and dried further. Smells faintly of a horse, which everybody mentions.

materials.name: Brahmi
materials.notes: Pulled by the handful from wet mud and used fresh, which limits it to where it grows.

materials.name: Haritaki
materials.notes: Dried until it rattles. Powdered it is a remedy and steeped it is the tannin that blacks a hide, and only the second of those is beyond dispute.

materials.name: Guggul
materials.notes: Tapped in beads from a cut in the bark. Smells like a temple and is swallowed like a pill.

materials.name: Pippali
materials.notes: Whole spikes picked unripe and dried grey. Hotter than round pepper and traded further.

items.name: Cordage
items.notes: The prototype every rope inherits from. Twisted fibre that holds two things together, and the single most useful object in this world by a distance nobody would guess.

items.name: Woven ware
items.notes: The prototype for mat, basket, sail and cloth -- one process at four scales, so one base with four overrides rather than four unrelated entities.

items.name: Blade
items.notes: The prototype for anything with a worked edge, before it is told what it is made of.

items.name: Hafted tool
items.notes: A head bound to a handle. The base for adze, pick and chisel: what they share is the binding, which is why cordage is a prerequisite of half the toolkit.

items.name: Vessel
items.notes: The prototype for anything that keeps something in. Distinct from `woven_ware`, whose job is to move a load rather than to hold one.

items.name: Prepared food
items.notes: The prototype for anything cooked, dried or pressed into a form somebody meant to eat later. A raw tuber and a baked one are different objects and only one is dinner.

items.name: Reed rope
items.notes: Light, cheap and rots. The house rope: everything that does not have to hold a boat.

items.name: Husk hawser
items.notes: Coarse palm-husk line that does not mind salt water. The harbour rope, and the reason a date palm is worth more standing than felled.

items.name: Sinew lashing
items.notes: Dries tight rather than merely holding, which is why every hafted tool wants it and no plant fibre will substitute.

items.name: Reed mat
items.notes: A floor, a wall, a roof or a bed depending on which way it is put down.

items.name: Carry basket
items.notes: Split cane ribs with reed weft. Carries as much as a person can and weighs almost nothing empty.

items.name: Fish weir
items.notes: A fence in the water that lets the river do the catching. Does not sort what it takes, which is why canon's fish material is named for the river and not for a species.

items.name: Goat-hair blanket
items.notes: Stays warm wet. On the Vindhya that is the only property anybody asks about.

items.name: Indigo cloth
items.notes: Comes out of the vat green and turns blue in the air while you watch. Half its worth is the colour and half is that everyone has seen it happen.

items.name: Sail cloth
items.notes: Coarse, heavy, and the difference between a boat that drifts and a boat that goes.

items.name: Flint knife
items.notes: Knapped in an afternoon, sharp for a week, replaced without ceremony.

items.name: Glass lancet
items.notes: Sharper than bronze and loses the edge to a hard look. Used where the cut matters more than the tool lasting -- surgery, and the finest carving.

items.name: Bronze knife
items.notes: Holds an edge, takes a new one, and is worth more than the person carrying it usually is.

items.name: Stone adze
items.notes: For dressing timber. The blade is set across the haft rather than along it, which is the whole difference between an adze and an axe and matters enormously to a boat.

items.name: Antler pick
items.notes: For clay, chalk and soft rock. Free, in the sense that the deer left it lying there.

items.name: Bronze chisel
items.notes: What dressed sandstone is dressed with. A settlement that has these has a mason.

items.name: Bone awl
items.notes: Bores a hole and scores a line. Filed under both cutting and marking because a tally is scratched with the same point that makes a stitch-hole.

items.name: Quern
items.notes: Grain to flour, ochre to pigment, bark to powder. The first object written here that had nothing honest to say for itself under the old vocabulary -- which is how `work` came to exist.

items.name: Bow drill
items.notes: Makes holes and makes fire, which is the same motion done with different patience.

items.name: Loom frame
items.notes: Upright, weighted, and taken apart to travel. Weaving needs a thing that works rather than a place that does, and this is that thing.

items.name: Bone harpoon
items.notes: The sawfish rostral tooth arrives already barbed, so this is a harpoon somebody did very little to. Canon says what it is for and pointedly not what it does to anything.

items.name: Reed spear
items.notes: Held level, it moves a herd. That is the whole of its recorded use.

items.name: Boar spear
items.notes: Cross-barred below the head so that what it stops does not walk up it. A defensive object described defensively, which is what canon has.

items.name: Bronze spearhead
items.notes: Socketed, so it outlives its shaft. Traded far past where anybody can make one.

items.name: Sling
items.notes: Two cords and a pouch. Affords only `deter`: canon records slings keeping birds off a crop far more often than it records them doing anything else.

items.name: Fire rattle
items.notes: Shells on a line, shaken. Filed as a weapon because that is honestly its category and it is the clearest case in the file that the category is not about harm.

items.name: Storage jar
items.notes: Fired, lidded, and half-buried to stay cool. A grain surplus is not a harvest, it is one of these.

items.name: Cooking pot
items.notes: Coarse-tempered so it survives the fire. Every cooked thing in canon passes through one.

items.name: Water skin
items.notes: Pitched inside. Tastes of it, and everyone stopped noticing generations ago.

items.name: Salt box
items.notes: Wood rather than clay, because salt draws water and a fired jar sweats.

items.name: Resin flask
items.notes: Small, stoppered, and worth more full than the room it sits in.

items.name: Grain bin
items.notes: Mud-plastered basketwork, taller than a person. Does not move once filled, which makes it the first object here that only a settlement can own.

items.name: Oil lamp
items.notes: A closed clay lamp with a shielded wick, the kind that survives being carried. Throws about an arm of light. **Varuna has carried one since the game's first step** -- canon is recording the kit rather than inventing it.

items.name: Reed torch
items.notes: Pitched reed bundle. Bright, brief, and gone in the rain.

items.name: Tinder bundle
items.notes: Kept dry against the body. The difference between a cold night and a warm one is usually whether somebody remembered this.

items.name: Brazier
items.notes: Portable fire. Lets a process that needs heat happen somewhere that has none.

items.name: Reed stylus
items.notes: Cut to a point and recut every few lines. Costs nothing and is lost constantly.

items.name: Ink cake
items.notes: Soot bound with gum, dried into a block, wetted on a stone. The substance Varuna's diary is actually written in.

items.name: Palm-leaf sheet
items.notes: Cut, boiled, dried and smoothed. Takes a scored line better than it takes ink.

items.name: Field diary
items.notes: Bound, and about a third full. **The game's whole progression system**: the crossings-out are the useful part, because a first guess is worth keeping once it is wrong. Affords marking alone. It holds writing, which is not what `contain` or `carry` mean.

items.name: Tally stick
items.notes: Notched and split, so both parties hold half and neither can add a notch alone. A contract that cannot be argued with.

items.name: Clay seal
items.notes: Pressed into the clay closing a jar or a bale. Says who packed it and that nobody has opened it since.

items.name: Flood bread
items.notes: Rice flour stretched with taro, which is what you eat in a year the rice did badly and the flood did well.

items.name: Dried fish
items.notes: Split, salted, racked. Keeps a season and travels anywhere.

items.name: Date block
items.notes: Pressed into a brick and wrapped in leaf. Sweet, heavy, and the reason a desert crossing is arithmetic rather than a gamble.

items.name: Tamarind paste
items.notes: Sour enough to make bad water drinkable and worse food interesting.

items.name: Salt-fish stew
items.notes: The pot everything ends up in. Nobody writes a recipe for it and everybody makes it.

items.name: Spiced rice
items.notes: The meal a settlement eats when there is nothing to mark.

items.name: Travel cake
items.notes: Rice flour, oil and fruit, baked hard. Made to be carried rather than to be enjoyed, and it tastes like it.

items.name: Mahua liquor
items.notes: Canon already records the tree for a fermented drink. Distilled nowhere -- this is the fermented thing itself, and strong enough.

items.name: Neem salve
items.notes: Bitter, oily, and keeps a wound clean. Canon has the tree for medicine already.

items.name: Myrrh poultice
items.notes: The wound salve canon names on the myrrh-thorn, softened in oil and spread on bast.

items.name: Shilajit tonic
items.notes: Scraped from high rock and taken in water. Worth carrying down the mountain, which is the only claim canon makes for it.

items.name: Bedroll
items.notes: Oiled cloth over a reed mat, rolled and strapped under the satchel. It has been rained on. **The game has carried this from its first step.** Affords shelter and nothing else: a bedroll strapped under a satchel is a thing being carried, not a thing that carries.

items.name: Hide tent
items.notes: Two people to raise and one to strike. What a caravan sleeps under when there is no travel node within a day.

items.name: Walking staff
items.notes: Shoulder height, worn smooth at the grip. Good for testing what will hold your weight before you stand on it. **Also from the game's kit.**

items.name: Mud shoes
items.notes: Splayed frames lashed under the foot. Cross a salt flat or a tidal mud that would otherwise take you to the knee.

items.name: Rope span
items.notes: A line fixed both banks, and a loop to hang from. Wants two people, which is why Teshk will not leave -- the rope needs two and there are not two to spare.

items.name: Shell bead
items.notes: Drilled, strung, and the smallest unit of worth anybody agrees on.

items.name: Ammonite pendant
items.notes: A spiral somebody found already made. The brown ones are worn; the Asura-marked black ones are not worn by anybody sensible.

items.name: Sandalwood comb
items.notes: Keeps its scent for a lifetime, which is most of why it is worth carrying anywhere.

items.name: The Fourteen
items.notes: Fourteen greens in one pot, bitter to the last, eaten on one night of the year. Nobody pretends it is pleasant, which is not what it is for.

items.name: Green mango sour
items.notes: Unripe mango, salted and dried on a mat. Sour enough to make bad water drinkable, which is what it is carried for.

items.name: Tempered oil
items.notes: Mustard oil taken to smoking and dropped over with seed, ginger and pod. Poured on at the end rather than cooked in, so what it carries is the smell. Affords carrying rather than containing: it is poured out of a flask, it is not the flask.

items.name: Green jackfruit pot
items.notes: Unripe jackfruit cooked long enough to pull apart in threads. It is not meat and the delta does not claim it is; it is what the tree gives a month before it gives sweets.

items.name: A grain of kuchla
items.notes: One purified seed ground into oil and divided into doses the size of a grain of rice. For a palsy, and for nothing else -- a preparation this specific is a preparation nobody improvises.

items.name: Ashwagandha tonic
items.notes: Root powder in warm oil, taken at night. For exhaustion, which canon distinguishes from illness.

items.name: Haritaki powder
items.notes: Dried fruit ground fine. Taken for almost anything, which is usually a sign a remedy does nothing in particular -- canon records the claim without endorsing it.

items.name: Guggul pill
items.notes: Resin softened and rolled with pepper. Worth carrying a long way, which is most of why the stands are overworked.

processes.name: Gathering
processes.notes: Picking a thing up. Named as a process rather than left implicit because every recipe chain has to start somewhere, and a layer whose raw materials arrive by magic cannot be checked for reachability.

processes.name: Knapping
processes.notes: Striking flakes off stone or glass to leave an edge. Wants nothing but a hammerstone and somewhere to sit, which is why it has no site and no needs.

processes.name: Retting
processes.notes: Rotting the soft parts off a stem in standing water until only fibre is left. Takes days and smells; done at the water's edge and never indoors.

processes.name: Spinning and twisting
processes.notes: Drawing fibre into thread, and thread into rope. The whorl is the tool and the tool is almost always somebody's spare moment.

processes.name: Weaving
processes.notes: Mat, basket, sail and cloth are one process at four scales. Needs a loom or a frame, which is a thing that works rather than a place that does.

processes.name: Carving
processes.notes: Shaping bone, wood, shell or antler with a blade. The most portable of the making processes -- it is what a person does at a camp fire with what they picked up that day.

processes.name: Tanning
processes.notes: Turning hide into leather with bark liquor and time. Sited at a settlement because it needs vats and because nobody will let you do it upwind of them.

processes.name: Firing
processes.notes: Clay to pottery in a kiln. The first process in this list that a person cannot do alone in a field, and the reason a settlement is worth walking back to.

processes.name: Smelting
processes.notes: Ore to metal. Needs a furnace, charcoal and somebody who has done it before. Canon is a bronze world, so this is near the edge of what anybody can do at all.

processes.name: Casting
processes.notes: Molten metal into a mould. Held apart from smelting because the skills are different and the failures are different.

processes.name: Pressing
processes.notes: Oil out of seed, under a beam or a stone. Wants a vessel to catch what comes out, which is the whole reason `contain` is a needed affordance and not a nicety.

processes.name: Grinding
processes.notes: Grain to flour, ochre to pigment, bark to powder. One quern does all three and the household that owns it does not lend it -- which is why this is sited: a saddle quern is two heavy stones that live somewhere, and nobody carries one.

processes.name: Cooking
processes.notes: Heat and a pot. Deliberately siteless -- a hearth is a fire somebody built, and a traveller builds one wherever they stop.

processes.name: Drying and salting
processes.notes: Preserving by taking the water out. Needs sun, air and patience, none of which canon models, so it needs nothing.

processes.name: Brewing
processes.notes: Fermenting. Canon already records the mahua for a fermented drink, so this process is describing something in the record rather than proposing an industry.

processes.name: Boatbuilding
processes.notes: Hull, frame, lashing and pitch. Sited at settlements and travel nodes because those are the two kinds of place in canon that sit on water and have people.

processes.name: Purifying
processes.notes:
Days of soaking, the liquor thrown away and replaced, and then drying. It is the one process here that adds nothing and removes something -- every other way of making turns a thing into more of a thing, and this turns a poison into a medicine by taking part of it away.

Slow on purpose and impossible to hurry, which is the whole safeguard: a preparation that could be rushed would be rushed.

recipes.name: Retting reed
recipes.notes: Nine days in standing water, then combed. The one recipe here that turns a thing into more of itself, because retting is what makes gathered reed into usable fibre at all.

recipes.name: Twisting reed rope
recipes.notes: Four handfuls to a working length. Wants a whorl, which is any item that works.

recipes.name: Laying a husk hawser
recipes.notes: Heavier and slower than reed, and it will still be there next season.

recipes.name: Drying sinew lashing
recipes.notes: Split, wetted and wound on while damp. Tightens as it dries, which is the whole point.

recipes.name: Weaving a reed mat
recipes.notes: Any fibre will do, which is what a tag ingredient is for -- reed in the delta, husk on the coast, and the recipe does not have to know which.

recipes.name: Weaving a carry basket
recipes.notes: Split cane ribs, then any fibre for the weft.

recipes.name: Setting a fish weir
recipes.notes: Built in the water and left. What it catches is not sorted, which is why the fish it gives is named for the river.

recipes.name: Weaving a blanket
recipes.notes: Known on the steppe and in the hills, where staying warm wet is the only question.

recipes.name: Dyeing indigo cloth
recipes.notes: Green out of the vat, blue in the air. Half its worth is that everyone has watched it happen.

recipes.name: Weaving sail cloth
recipes.notes: Coarse and heavy. The difference between a boat that drifts and a boat that goes.

recipes.name: Knapping a flint knife
recipes.notes: An afternoon's work, sharp for a week, replaced without ceremony.

recipes.name: Knapping a glass lancet
recipes.notes: Magma-glass or scar-glass, whichever the ground offers -- they knap the same, which is why they share a class.

recipes.name: Hafting a stone adze
recipes.notes: The blade set across the haft, not along it. That difference matters enormously to a boat.

recipes.name: Hafting an antler pick
recipes.notes: Free, in the sense that the deer left it lying there.

recipes.name: Carving a bone awl
recipes.notes: Bores a hole and scores a line, with the same point.

recipes.name: Making a bow drill
recipes.notes: Holes and fire, the same motion at different patience.

recipes.name: Building a loom frame
recipes.notes: Upright, weighted, taken apart to travel. Every woven thing waits on this one.

recipes.name: Dressing a quern
recipes.notes: Two stones, dressed to sit true. The household that owns one does not lend it.

recipes.name: Cutting a walking staff
recipes.notes: Shoulder height, worn smooth at the grip in its own time.

recipes.name: Lashing mud shoes
recipes.notes: Splayed frames under the foot. A salt flat becomes ground you can cross.

recipes.name: Notching a tally
recipes.notes: Notched and split so both halves must agree. A contract nobody can argue with.

recipes.name: Carving a comb
recipes.notes: Keeps its scent for a lifetime, which is most of why anyone carries one.

recipes.name: Drilling shell beads
recipes.notes: The smallest unit of worth anybody agrees on, and Harappa is where they are made.

recipes.name: Drilling an ammonite
recipes.notes: A spiral somebody found already made.

recipes.name: Binding a bone harpoon
recipes.notes: The rostral tooth arrives barbed. Very little is done to it.

recipes.name: Binding a reed spear
recipes.notes: Held level, it moves a herd. That is its recorded use.

recipes.name: Binding a boar spear
recipes.notes: Cross-barred below the head, so that what it stops does not walk up it.

recipes.name: Braiding a sling
recipes.notes: Two cords and a pouch. Keeps birds off a crop far more often than anything else.

recipes.name: Stringing a fire rattle
recipes.notes: Shells on a line. The clearest case in canon that a weapon is not about harm.

recipes.name: Crushing grog
recipes.notes: Old fired pots, crushed back into new clay so the new one survives the kiln. The only material in canon that can only be made out of itself.

recipes.name: Firing a storage jar
recipes.notes: A grain surplus is not a harvest. It is one of these.

recipes.name: Firing a cooking pot
recipes.notes: Coarse-tempered so it survives the fire it is made for.

recipes.name: Firing an oil lamp
recipes.notes: A closed lamp with a shielded wick, the kind that survives being carried.

recipes.name: Firing a brazier
recipes.notes: Portable fire. Lets heat happen where there is none.

recipes.name: Cutting a seal
recipes.notes: Says who packed it and that nobody has opened it since.

recipes.name: Firing a resin flask
recipes.notes: Small, stoppered, worth more full than the room it sits in.

recipes.name: Raising a grain bin
recipes.notes: Mud-plastered basketwork, taller than a person. Does not move once filled -- the first object here only a settlement can own.

recipes.name: Burning charcoal
recipes.notes: Burnt slow under turf. The only fuel hot enough to melt anything.

recipes.name: Boiling pitch
recipes.notes: In a covered pit. Nothing floats without it.

recipes.name: Making a torch
recipes.notes: Bright, brief, and gone in the rain.

recipes.name: Making tinder
recipes.notes: Kept dry against the body. Usually the difference between a cold night and a warm one.

recipes.name: Tanning hide
recipes.notes: Bark liquor and time. Nobody will let you do it upwind of them.

recipes.name: Pitching a water skin
recipes.notes: Tastes of the pitch. Everyone stopped noticing generations ago.

recipes.name: Making a bedroll
recipes.notes: Oiled cloth over a reed mat. It has been rained on.

recipes.name: Raising a hide tent
recipes.notes: Two people to raise and one to strike.

recipes.name: Fixing a rope span
recipes.notes: A line fixed both banks and a loop to hang from. Wants two people, which is why Teshk will not leave.

recipes.name: Carving a salt box
recipes.notes: Wood rather than clay, because salt draws water and a fired jar sweats.

recipes.name: Smelting copper
recipes.notes: Canon is a bronze world with iron as a rumour. Nothing above this line goes further.

recipes.name: Casting bronze
recipes.notes: Copper and tin. Worth more than the person carrying it usually is.

recipes.name: Casting a bronze knife
recipes.notes: Holds an edge and takes a new one.

recipes.name: Casting a chisel
recipes.notes: What dressed sandstone is dressed with. A settlement with these has a mason.

recipes.name: Casting a spearhead
recipes.notes: Socketed, so it outlives its shaft. Traded far past where anyone can make one.

recipes.name: Grinding ochre
recipes.notes: Ground and washed. The oldest pigment anybody has.

recipes.name: Catching lamp black
recipes.notes: Soot on a cold plate held over a flame.

recipes.name: Fermenting indigo
recipes.notes: Stinks for a fortnight. Then it is worth what it is worth.

recipes.name: Pressing an ink cake
recipes.notes: Soot bound with gum and dried into a block. What Varuna's diary is written in.

recipes.name: Cutting a stylus
recipes.notes: Recut every few lines, and lost constantly.

recipes.name: Preparing palm leaf
recipes.notes: Cut, boiled, dried, smoothed. Takes a scored line better than it takes ink.

recipes.name: Binding a field diary
recipes.notes: The crossings-out are the useful part. A first guess is worth keeping once it is wrong.

recipes.name: Pressing mahua oil
recipes.notes: Under a beam or a stone, with something underneath to catch it.

recipes.name: Grinding flour
recipes.notes: Any grain. The quern does not care and neither does the recipe.

recipes.name: Baking flood bread
recipes.notes: What you eat in a year the rice did badly and the flood did well.

recipes.name: Drying fish
recipes.notes: Split, salted, racked. Keeps a season and travels anywhere.

recipes.name: Pressing a date block
recipes.notes: Wrapped in leaf. Why a desert crossing is arithmetic rather than a gamble.

recipes.name: Making tamarind paste
recipes.notes: Sour enough to make bad water drinkable and worse food interesting.

recipes.name: Cooking salt-fish stew
recipes.notes: The pot everything ends up in. Nobody writes it down and everybody makes it.

recipes.name: Cooking spiced rice
recipes.notes: What a settlement eats when there is nothing to mark.

recipes.name: Baking travel cake
recipes.notes: Baked hard. Made to be carried rather than enjoyed, and it tastes like it.

recipes.name: Brewing mahua
recipes.notes: Fermented, not distilled. Strong enough.

recipes.name: Making neem salve
recipes.notes: Bitter, oily, keeps a wound clean.

recipes.name: Making a myrrh poultice
recipes.notes: The salve canon already names on the thorn, spread on bast.

recipes.name: Preparing shilajit
recipes.notes: Scraped from high rock and taken in water.

recipes.name: Cooking the fourteen
recipes.notes: Fourteen, counted. A cook who is one short does not make it with thirteen -- they go back out.

recipes.name: Salting green mango
recipes.notes: Sliced, salted and left on a mat in the sun for four days.

recipes.name: Tempering oil
recipes.notes: Oil taken to smoking, then seed and pod dropped in off the heat. Poured over at the end.

recipes.name: Cooking green jackfruit
recipes.notes: Cooked until it pulls apart in threads. Hands are oiled first or the sap will not come off.

recipes.name: Pressing mustard oil
recipes.notes: A second oil for the delta, and a hotter one. Canon keeps one oil material -- what changes is which seed the press was fed.

recipes.name: Purifying kuchla
recipes.notes: A fortnight of soaking, the liquor thrown away and replaced daily. **The only kind of recipe that consumes a poison in canon**, and that is deliberate rather than an omission: there is no word in `affordances.json` for what a thing made to harm somebody would be for.

recipes.name: Dividing a dose
recipes.notes: Ground into oil and divided small. The dividing is the safeguard and is done in company.

recipes.name: Making a tonic
recipes.notes: Warmed, not boiled. Taken at night.

recipes.name: Grinding haritaki
recipes.notes: Dried until it rattles, then ground fine enough to float.

recipes.name: Rolling guggul
recipes.notes: Softened over heat and rolled between the palms with pepper.

vehicles.name: Reed raft
vehicles.notes: Bundled reed lashed to a cane frame. Rots in a season and is rebuilt in a morning, which is the correct trade for something that only has to cross a channel.

vehicles.name: Dugout
vehicles.notes: One trunk, burnt and adzed hollow. The adze blade set across the haft rather than along it is the whole reason this is possible.

vehicles.name: Coracle
vehicles.notes: A basket with a skin over it. Spins constantly, carries far more than it should, and one person can walk home with it on their back.

vehicles.name: Delta barge
vehicles.notes: Flat-bottomed and poled. What actually moves a grain surplus, and therefore what a settlement is downstream of in every sense.

vehicles.name: Coastal dhow
vehicles.notes: Sewn rather than nailed -- husk cordage through drilled planks, and the whole hull flexes. Canon records iron-teak for ship timber, and this is what it is for.

vehicles.name: Outrigger
vehicles.notes: A hull too narrow to stand up on its own, and a float that makes it the steadiest thing on open water. The Kelpfang is one of these, grown rather than built.

vehicles.name: Ox cart
vehicles.notes: Solid wheels, no springs, and a pace nobody hurries. Carries what a barge cannot reach.

vehicles.name: Salt sled
vehicles.notes: Dragged over a salt pan where a wheel would cut through the crust and stop. Dwarka's answer to ground that is neither water nor road.

vehicles.name: Bone-framed trawler
vehicles.notes: Canon states the Abyssal Blue's bone plate is harvested for building maritime vessels. This is that claim made into a ship: a single rib is a keel, and the Leviathan's Rib is the one canon names.

vehicles.name: Ground-effect craft
vehicles.notes: Flies a few metres above the water and cannot go higher, which makes it neither a boat nor an aircraft and useless anywhere but the open Tethys. The Battered Ekranoplan is the one canon has, bought cheap off delta salvagers.

vehicles.name: Workshop train
vehicles.notes: A travelling apothecary and workshop rather than transport. The Survival Train gathers the displaced across the broken country, which is a use for a vehicle that has nothing to do with getting anywhere.

vehicles.name: Harappan cart
vehicles.notes:
Two solid wheels of three planks dowelled together, and an axle that turns with them rather than under them -- so the whole undercarriage groans and a driver is heard coming from a field away. Nobody has improved on it because nothing about it is difficult: a household can cut one, and a broken wheel is three new planks.

The commonest vehicle in canon and the least remarked on, which is the usual fate of the thing everybody has. It is drawn in miniature more often than it is written about -- small clay carts turn up in every settlement, in numbers that make more sense as toys than as votives, though canon does not insist on either.

vehicles.name: The Sinauli wagon
vehicles.notes:
Copper-sheathed along every edge a hand would touch, with triangular figures worked into the wheel faces. Found only in graves, and only ever with a body in it.

**Canon files it as a cart, and the argument is the point.** Its wheels are solid -- three planks and a copper rim, the same construction as the household cart above -- and a spoked wheel is what would make it a chariot. So the people who bury one are burying something that looks like a war machine and is built like a farm vehicle, and canon does not know which of those they meant. Recording the dispute rather than settling it is the same call made about the Shattering: the question is better than any answer available.
